cards.front: Normal pCO₂ range: [___] mmHg.
cards.context: CO₂ is volatile acid — retained by hypoventilation (respiratory acidosis) or blown off by hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis). The lungs respond within minutes to compensate for metabolic disturbances.

cards.front: Tourniquets are safe for up to [___] hours; always document time of application.
cards.context:
The 2-hour tourniquet window comes from military trauma data: ischaemic nerve injury and reperfusion complications are rare under 2 hours, increase between 2-6 hours, and become common beyond 6.

The time-of-application written on the tourniquet (or limb) is critical for downstream decisions: short interval = release once volume-resuscitated and bleeding controlled by other.

The bigger error is hesitating to apply one when needed — uncontrolled extremity haemorrhage is rapidly fatal.

cards.front: NAC can cease when paracetamol is <10 mg/L, ALT is falling, INR is <[___], and the patient is asymptomatic; pH belongs to King's College transplant criteria.
cards.context:
NAC cessation criteria are conservative because hepatotoxicity peaks at 72-96 hours and can still progress after NAC is stopped.

King's College Hospital criteria for paracetamol-induced acute liver failure (the threshold for transplant referral) include: arterial pH <7.3 after fluid resuscitation, OR all three of (creatinine >300 µmol/L.

cards.front: Ampicillin is added to urinary sepsis regimens because ceftriaxone misses [___].
cards.context: Gentamicin covers Gram-negatives (E. coli, Klebsiella), ampicillin adds Enterococcus coverage. Ceftriaxone is an alternative for Gram-negatives but misses Enterococcus — check local protocols.

cards.front: Anaphylaxis can occur without [___] features if hypotension, bronchospasm, or upper airway obstruction is present.
cards.context:
ASCIA provides the Australian definition. Key point: anaphylaxis can occur WITHOUT typical skin features if hypotension, bronchospasm, or upper airway obstruction is present.

If in doubt, always treat for anaphylaxis.

cards.front: Estimated total blood volume in an adult is about [___] mL/kg of ideal body weight.
cards.context:
To apply the 'half blood volume in 4h' trigger you need the patient's blood volume. Estimate it as ~70 mL/kg of IDEAL body weight (not actual — fat is poorly vascularised).

Worked example: a 95 kg, 1.6 m patient has IBW ≈ 22 × 1.6² ≈ 56 kg, so blood volume ≈ 56 × 70 mL ≈ 3.9 L (and 'half in 4h' ≈ 2 L).

cards.front: Ottawa Ankle Rules: X-ray if tenderness at posterior lateral or medial malleolus (distal 6 cm), base of 5th metatarsal, navicular bone, or unable to [___] 4 steps.
cards.context: The Ottawa rules check four bony areas plus weight-bearing ability. The midfoot component (base of 5th MT and navicular) is often forgotten but catches important fractures that can be missed clinically.

cards.front: Adult acute asthma steroid dose is prednisone 37.5–50 mg PO (unlike paediatric, it is not [___]-based).
cards.context: Adult treatment for the same severity is very similar — burst salbutamol and ipratropium via spacer, with prednisone dose of 37.5–50 mg instead of weight-based.

cards.front: Acute respiratory acidosis: HCO₃ rises [___] per 10 mmHg ΔpCO₂. Chronic: rises 3.5.
cards.context:
Acute respiratory compensation takes hours with small HCO₃ shifts. Chronic compensation (3–5 days) allows larger renal adjustment.

Values are per 10 mmHg change in pCO₂.

cards.front: For community-acquired intra-abdominal sepsis (anaerobe cover needed, no MRSA risk), first-line empiric antibiotics are [___] + metronidazole.
cards.context: Community-acquired intra-abdominal sepsis: source = abdomen (below diaphragm = anaerobe cover needed), community-acquired, no MRSA risk. Ceftriaxone covers community Gram-negatives, metronidazole covers anaerobes.

cards.front: A patient with melaena has urea 12 mmol/L (normal <7) but creatinine 80 µmol/L (normal <110); the disproportionately high urea localises the bleed to the [___] GI tract.
cards.context:
Digested blood is absorbed in the small bowel as a protein load, raising urea production; the kidney is unaffected so creatinine stays normal.

A high urea-to-creatinine ratio in a patient with melaena therefore localises the bleed proximally — a classic interpretation trap.

cards.front: RSTI NAC thresholds: paracetamol >[___] mg/L OR ALT >50 U/L. The nomogram does NOT apply to RSTI.
cards.context: RSTI management differs from acute overdose — the nomogram doesn't apply. Instead, use screening labs and clinical criteria to guide NAC.

cards.front: CRASH-2 showed TXA benefit only within 3 hours of injury; after this window there is possible [___].
cards.context:
CRASH-2 (2010, 20,000 trauma patients) found tranexamic acid (1 g over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 hours) reduces all-cause mortality and bleeding deaths if given within 3 hours of injury.

After 3 hours, TXA may HARM — possibly through paradoxical bleeding from secondary fibrinolysis activation. Document time of injury, not time of presentation. Don't give TXA late.

cards.front: In RSTI, no NAC is needed if ALT <[___] AND paracetamol <20 mg/L.
cards.context: In RSTI, if ALT is under 50 AND paracetamol level is under 20 mg/L, no NAC treatment is needed. Otherwise commence NAC.

cards.front: Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back with >20 mmHg BP difference between arms suggests [___].
cards.context:
Aortic dissection: sudden 'tearing'/'ripping' chest/back pain reaching maximum intensity at onset (unlike MI which crescendos).

Workup: bilateral BP, focused echo if Type A suspected (AR, pericardial effusion, intimal flap), then CT aortogram.

cards.front: Post-ROSC, target SpO₂ 94–98% to avoid [___], which worsens neurological outcomes via free radical injury.
cards.context:
Post-ROSC the brain is in a vulnerable reperfusion state — every excess oxygen molecule generates reactive oxygen species (superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, hydroxyl radical) that compound the original ischaemic injury.

SpO₂ 94-98% (titrate FiO₂ down from 1.0 once SpO₂ confirmed reliable) is the post-arrest standard. Same principle applies to neonatal resus: use room air or low FiO₂, escalate only if SpO₂ targets are missed.

cards.front: PCA background infusions increase risk of [___] without improving outcomes. Monitor RR/SpO₂ hourly for first 6-12 hours.
cards.context:
PCA allows patient autonomy over opioid dosing. Background infusions are NOT routinely used — they don't improve outcomes and increase respiratory depression risk.

Monitoring is critical: hourly for first 6-12 hours, then 2-hourly.

cards.front: Dual antiplatelet therapy after TIA is indicated when ABCD² score is ≥ [___]; the loading dose of aspirin is 300 mg.
cards.context:
ABCD² ≥4 = high early-stroke-risk TIA. Add clopidogrel to aspirin for 21 days (CHANCE / POINT trials) — DAPT reduces 90-day stroke risk by ~30% compared with aspirin alone.

ABCD² components: Age ≥60 (1), BP ≥140/90 (1), Clinical (unilateral weakness 2 / speech 1 / other 0), Duration (≥60 min 2 / 10-59 1), Diabetes (1).

cards.front: Bronchodilator reversibility requires BOTH >12% AND >[___] mL improvement in FEV1; failure to meet this in an obstructive pattern suggests COPD over asthma.
cards.context:
Significant bronchodilator reversibility = FEV₁ improvement of BOTH ≥12% AND ≥200 mL after salbutamol — the dual criterion prevents a small absolute change in a low FEV₁ from looking impressive in percentage terms.

Reversibility favours asthma; non-reversible obstruction suggests COPD. But the test is imperfect: ~30% of asthmatics fail to reverse on a given day, and ~10% of COPD patients show partial reversibility.

cards.front: In the WHO 6-step prescribing model, jumping from diagnosis to treatment skips Step 2: specifying the [___] objective.
cards.context:
WHO Guide to Good Prescribing breaks the act into six steps: define problem, specify therapeutic objective, choose treatment, write prescription, give information/warnings, monitor and review.

Naming the objective forces a useful pause. 'Treating the pneumonia' becomes 'clear bacterial infection in 5-7 days while avoiding C. difficile and renal injury' — that reframes antibiotic selection, duration.

cards.front: In variceal bleeding, target Hb 70-80 g/L; over-transfusion raises [___] pressure and rebleeding risk.
cards.context:
Variceal bleeding is the one setting where transfusing 'more, sooner' actively kills.

Unique to portal hypertensive bleeding (in ACS or trauma the balance tips back to higher targets).

cards.front: In the SLICE protocol (Sick patient, Lungs, IVC, Cardiac, Extras), dry lungs (A-lines) + collapsing IVC = likely hypovolaemic/distributive shock. Action: [___].
cards.context:
SLICE is a structured bedside ultrasound for shock workup in <60 seconds — Sick patient, Lungs (A-lines vs B-lines), IVC (collapsibility), Cardiac (function + pericardium), Extras (FAST, AAA, DVT).

A-lines = dry alveoli; collapsing IVC = low RA pressure. Together: volume-depleted (or vasodilated) — fluids safe and likely helpful.

cards.front: Young patients maintain BP until [___]% blood loss, then decompensate rapidly.
cards.context: Young patients compensate extremely well with tachycardia and vasoconstriction — they maintain BP until they've lost 30% of blood volume, then crash suddenly.

cards.front: Propofol for refractory status epilepticus: [___] mg/kg bolus then 1-5 mg/kg/hr infusion.
cards.context:
Refractory status (failure of two anti-seizure agents) requires general anaesthesia to break the seizure — without it, ongoing electrical activity causes irreversible excitotoxic neuronal injury within hours.

Patient needs intubation (no longer protecting airway), continuous EEG, ICU admission. Watch for propofol infusion syndrome at high doses or prolonged use; consider switching to midazolam or thiopentone if running >48 h.

cards.front: The temperature threshold defining fever for blood culture indications is ≥[___]°C, not 37.5°C.
cards.context:
Fever threshold matters for blood culture indications. 37.5 degrees is NOT fever — the CEC threshold is 38 degrees or above.

Hypothermia (36 degrees or below) also counts as a SIRS criterion.

cards.front: In ACS with SBP below 100 mmHg, opioids should be [___] until haemodynamics are optimised.
cards.context:
Opioids in ACS work for pain but at the cost of preload and afterload.

Hierarchy in hypotensive ACS: fix haemodynamics first (IV fluids if RV-dependent inferior MI, vasopressors if cardiogenic shock), then revisit analgesia.

cards.front: ATS Category 3 (potentially life-threatening) has a maximum wait time of [___] minutes.
cards.context:
ATS Category 3 covers conditions that are potentially life- or limb-threatening if treatment is significantly delayed — moderate-severity asthma, sepsis without shock, moderate haemorrhage, suspected DKA.

Achieving the target requires a free assessment bay; failure usually reflects ED overcrowding rather than triage error.

cards.front: In bacterial meningitis, give dexamethasone 10 mg IV with or just [___] the first antibiotic dose — but never delay antibiotics to give it.
cards.context:
Bacterial lysis from the first antibiotic dose dumps a wall of inflammatory cell-wall fragments into the CSF, driving the worst of the meningeal inflammation, cerebral oedema, and hearing loss.

Given after antibiotics have already lysed the bacteria, dexamethasone misses its window — the inflammation is already triggered.

cards.front: Preferred imaging for suspected appendicitis in pregnancy or children is [___].
cards.context:
Ultrasound avoids ionising radiation — critical in pregnancy (teratogenic risk to fetus) and paediatrics (lifetime cumulative-dose risk).

So if USS is negative but clinical suspicion remains, escalate to MRI in pregnancy (no radiation) or low-dose CT in children. Adults default to CT first-line (>95% sensitivity, fast).
